newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat says Israeli measures a declaration of war.
newsitem.headline: Arafat says Israeli measures a declaration of war.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Saturday accused Israel of declaring war on his people over its security clampdown after this week's suicide bombings in Jerusalem.

As Israel put more police on its streets for fear of further attacks, Arafat said measures taken by Israel to prevent any infiltration of Islamic militants from Palestinian areas were an excuse to "chain" the peace process.

"The Israeli government used this situation and this incident to declare war on the Palestinian people, their National Authority and their leadership instead of declaring it against terrorism," Arafat said.
He told reporters after talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak that it was now more crucial than ever for U.S. President Bill Clinton to intervene to save the Middle East peace process.

Wednesday's twin suicide bombing in Jerusalem's main Jewish market killed 15 people including the two attackers and plunged Arafat's already frosty relations with Israel's right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to an all-time low.

Netanyahu, elected last year on a pledge to keep Israel safe from attack, has accused the Palestinian leader of doing "damn all" to control Moslem militants opposed to the Jewish state's existence and Israeli-Palestinian peace deals.

He has suspended peace talks, sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip and signalled that he would send forces into areas handed over to Palestinian self-rule to seize militants if Arafat fails to do the job.

Israel's neighbour Jordan said on Saturday that it was worried that the Israeli clampdown went beyond tackling legitimate security concerns, warning that a heavy hand in battling militants "will only lead to more tension".
Foreign Minister Fayez al-Tarawanah said Israel had to perceive Arafat as a partner rather than a foe.
"We say Israel has to consider the Palestinian Authority as a partner and not as an enemy or adversary and the security issue has to be viewed within that perspective," Tarawnah told reporters.
Wednesday's twin bombings were the bloodiest in Israel for well over a year.

Responsibility was claimed in a leaflet issued in the name of the militant Islamic resistance movement Hamas which included an ultimatum to Israel to release all Palestinian prisoners by nine p.m. (1800 GMT) on Sunday night.

Israeli police spokeswoman Linda Menuhin said the ultimatum in the leaflet, whose authenticity has not been fully established, was one factor in Saturday's decision to increase the number of police on patrol in Israel's towns and cities.

She said Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani and police chief Assaf Hefetz had decided to "reinforce police forces in crowded areas", strengthen security along borders with the West Bank and Gaza Strip and set up more checkpoints.
Islamic militants have in the past carried out suicide bombings in waves, killing 57 people in February and March 1996 in a series of attacks.
Wednesday's bombings came on the eve of a planned visit to the region by U.S. envoy Dennis Ross after cautious signs that four months of stagnation in Israeli-PLO peace talks might be about to end.

Ross's trip was immediately postponed but Clinton said on Friday that it would take place once Israel had mourned its dead, possibly as a prelude to a maiden visit by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
The teetering peace process stalled in March when Israel broke ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, which it occupied in the 1967 Middle East War.
Arafat has insisted on a freeze in settlement building as a condition for substantive peace talks. Netanyahu says movement cannot come unless the Palestinian Authority acts on security.

"There is no other issue than security at this point and if Ross succeeds in getting the Palestinians to move on this issue there is hope for the peace process," Netanyahu's communications chief, David Bar-Illan, told Reuters.

The crisis has broken as Arafat seeks to shore up his popular legitimacy following mounting resentment among Palestinians over alleged corruption and mismanagement by some of his ministers and Palestinian Authority officials.

All but two members of the 18-strong cabinet offered to resign on Friday after a scathing report by Palestinian legislators but Arafat signalled on Saturday that he would not act on the gesture in present circumstances.
"This is still (a) long period (away)," he said in English.
